cosy-lesson.title: Brain Cells That Keep You Motivated (B1)

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Motivation ≠ apathy – the reason or desires that compel someone to act.

p.em: Example: Scientists discovered brain cells that control daily motivation.

cosy-blockquote.p: Neuron ≠ blood cell – a specialized cell transmitting nerve impulses; a nerve cell.

p.em: Example: Specific neural circuits fire when we initiate a tough task.

cosy-blockquote.p: Circuit ≠ fragment – a neural pathway in the brain.

p.em: Example: Dopamine circuits regulate feelings of reward and drive.

cosy-blockquote.p: Perseverance ≠ surrender – persistence in doing something despite difficulty.

p.em: Example: Brain cells dedicated to perseverance help us finish long projects.

cosy-blockquote.p: Dopamine ≠ cortisol – a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and motivation.

p.em: Example: Dopamine release encourages repeated goal-oriented behavior.

cosy-blockquote.p: Discharge ≠ accumulation – the firing or release of electrical activity in neurons.

p.em: Example: Neuronal discharge increases when a reward is near.

cosy-blockquote.p: Incentive ≠ deterrent – a thing that motivates or encourages one to do something.

p.em: Example: Clear incentives activate brain circuits for action.

cosy-blockquote.p: Fatigue ≠ vigor – extreme tiredness resulting from mental or physical exertion.

p.em: Example: Overcoming mental fatigue depends on specific cell signaling.

cosy-blockquote.p: Stimulus ≠ inertia – a thing or event that evokes a specific functional reaction.

p.em: Example: A positive stimulus triggers neural drive to achieve goals.

cosy-blockquote.p: Initiative ≠ passivity – the ability to assess and initiate things independently.

p.em: Example: Taking initiative requires strong neural activation.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
How does intrinsic motivation drive long-term academic and professional success?
★ What project recently gave you a strong surge of motivation?

What is the basic function of a neuron in transmitting chemical messages?
★ Did you enjoy learning biology at school?

How does a neural circuit process external rewards and form daily habits?
★ What good daily habit have you built recently?

Why is psychological perseverance essential when tackling difficult challenges?
★ How do you handle failure or unexpected setbacks?

What role does dopamine release play in feeling satisfaction after completing a task?
★ What simple activities give you a quick feeling of accomplishment?

How does an electrical discharge between neurons create sensory experiences?
★ Are you interested in brain science discoveries?

What financial or personal incentive encourages you to work harder?
★ What reward system works best for your personal goals?

How do you manage physical and mental fatigue after a hectic workday?
★ What is your favorite way to restore your energy levels?

How does a positive visual stimulus trigger creative thinking in the brain?
★ What environment inspires your best ideas?

Why is taking personal initiative important in modern competitive workplaces?
★ Do you prefer starting new projects or managing existing ones?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Look at the prompt and discuss your response with your teacher:

cosy-blockquote.p: A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Sustained personal motivation depends more on structured habits than on fleeting emotions. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you rely on self-discipline or mood?

Mapping every human neuron will allow scientists to cure procrastination. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you participate in brain mapping studies?

Rewiring a bad neural circuit takes at least one month of consistent practice. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Have you successfully broken a bad habit?

Grittiness and perseverance predict lifelong success better than high IQ score. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Value hard work or raw talent more?

Excessive digital stimulation overuses our dopamine pathways and reduces real-world joy. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Have you ever tried a digital detox?

Measuring neural discharge in real-time will change how we diagnose mental fatigue. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you wear a smartwatch that monitors brain strain?

Financial incentive alone is insufficient to keep employees truly engaged. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Value workplace culture over higher salary?

Overcoming chronic fatigue requires fundamental changes in sleep schedule and nutrition. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ How many hours of sleep do you average?

Responding constructively to a stressful stimulus is a mark of high emotional intelligence. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Keep calm under pressure?

Taking individual initiative should be rewarded more than following routine instructions. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Encourage proactive decision-making at work?

ul.li: Incorrect: The cells who control motivation. → Correct: The cells which / that control motivation. ((Use 'which' or 'that' for non-human objects and cells, not 'who'.))
Incorrect: Dopamine make us feels good. → Correct: Dopamine makes us feel good. ((Causative verb 'make' takes base verb without '-s': 'makes us feel'.))
